claims.claim: lake outlets run warm: natural lakes raised outlet streams by 3.4 °C in southern Quebec (Auffray et al. 2023, abstract)
claims.note: Article not read (the paper itself marks it 'abstract'). The abstract (EspaceINRS record): 'In August 2020, we observed an average warming of 3.7 °C downstream of reservoirs … the warming effect of reservoirs was not significantly different from the warming effect of natural lakes (3.4 °C)'. The stand-in thesis (read in full; Chapter II, printed pp. 18–28, PDF pp. 26–36) gives the conditions, which the rewrite should carry: the 3.4 °C is the mean difference in AUGUST-MEAN water temperature (Mmo8) between the main inflowing tributary and the outlet stream, with the outlet sensor 'le plus proche possible de l'exutoire', in August 2020 only, for FOUR small natural lakes in Gatineau Park (Kelly 27.4 ha, Lusk 33.4, Kidder 5.8, Meunier 1.9; Table 1, printed p. 19); SD 2.9 °C, range 0.4 °C (Lusk) to 6.7 °C (Kelly) (printed pp. 27–28: 'un réchauffement moyen de 3,4 °C (écart-type = 2,9 °C)'). Five lakes were instrumented; sensor failures left four. Below the lakes the mean daily range fell by 2.2 °C. The thesis supports the paper's wording if it adds 'in August, below four small lakes (2–33 ha)'.

notes: Recommend citing the thesis for the numbers (Auffray, M. 2021. M.Sc. thesis, Université du Québec en Outaouais, di.uqo.ca eprint 1356), or keep 'Auffray et al. 2023' and add the conditions above. Other values in the thesis that bear on the brook below Upper: reservoirs (surface-release dams under 4 m) warmed their outlets by 3.7 °C (SD 2.2) in August 2020; distance to an upstream water body, drainage area and the share of the watershed in water bodies were the main predictors of August stream temperature in a GAM; the 25 °C threshold used is brook trout's critical maximum (Hasnain et al. 2010). The lakes are small lakes in Gatineau Park, a 361-km² protected area of mostly deciduous forest on the Canadian Shield (printed p. 16); their depths and whether they stratify are not given in Table 1, and the warming depended strongly on the lake (0.4 to 6.7 °C), so 3.4 °C is not a transferable constant for Upper Hot Brook Lake's outlet.
